prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: After reading the eight opening ballots I still put IceCube first. A cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice found astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, a new observational window on the universe. The result survived the hard part, which is background control: atmospheric muons and atmospheric neutrinos were rejected, and the same excess appeared in several independent analysis channels, so this is not a single-analysis claim. It also bears on the century-old question of where cosmic rays come from, and the later TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results show the window is productive rather than a one-off. Halzen conceived and drove the cubic-kilometre concept and Karle was central to construction and the discovery analyses, so a two-name prize is clean. The physics is not the kind that will be overturned. No other shortlisted entry combines a new window, decisive instrument work and independent confirmation as clearly.
statement.case_against: My own reservation is that I am an astroparticle experimentalist, so this is close to my taste and I may overrate it. Substantively, the source identifications rest largely on one experiment and KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD have not yet independently confirmed them, so I would cite only the diffuse flux. The attribution is also not as tidy as the two-name list suggests. The AMANDA predecessor, other IceCube leaders and the key analysts could all claim a decisive role, and I cannot settle that split from the supplied text. A fair committee should recognise that the strongest competitor on breadth of support is the Katori-Ye optical lattice clock, which five of eight members ranked, whereas IceCube has only two first-place votes. If the committee wants a consensus candidate, B045 is probably it.

responses.point: Ranked B016 first as a genuinely new window on the universe with a clear observable and a purpose-built instrument, while noting that the split of decisive credit between Halzen, Karle and other IceCube or Antarctic pioneers is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree on the merit and share the attribution worry. Where I would go further is on citation wording. We should credit the diffuse-flux discovery, which has been confirmed in multiple channels, and not the source identifications, which still depend largely on one detector. That narrows the claim and also narrows the attribution dispute to the people who made the detection possible, namely the concept and construction leadership and the analysis that separated the astrophysical flux from atmospheric backgrounds. Please say whether you would be comfortable with a citation that does not mention TXS 0506+056.

responses.point: Ranked B045 first as the measurement breakthrough he values most, with 1e-18 uncertainty, relativistic geodesy and a route to redefining the second, and with confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST. He flags the open distinction from the 2005 comb prize and Hall's laser stabilisation.
responses.response: I put B045 second and I take your case seriously, because the instrument-and-measurement logic is the same one I apply to IceCube. My qualification is on priority. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength idea, but the early strontium lattice demonstrations and the accuracy frontier are shared with other groups such as SYRTE, and the 2005 prize and Wineland's 2012 prize already cover combs and ion clocks. I do not think that is disqualifying, since the many-atom lattice clock is a distinct achievement, but it is the argument I would want a clock specialist to defend in detail. On the numbers you have the broader support, so I will not treat opening rank as merit, but it matters for consensus.

responses.point: Ranked B040 first as a general mechanism, a topological invariant protecting edge states, that reshaped how condensed matter is classified, and notes that the supplied credit excludes Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and that Hasan's three-dimensional work may need separate treatment.
responses.response: This is outside my field, so I rely on you and Eva Olsson. I do see a real attribution problem. You and Olsson proposed different three-person sets from the same four names (Mele in one, Hasan in the other), and the quantum spin Hall chain through HgTe has a theory step by people outside the list. If the committee cannot settle who the decisive three are, that weakens a prize even when the science is clearly lasting. I would want the condensed-matter members to say which two- or three-person set they can all defend, and whether two-dimensional and three-dimensional topological insulators are one achievement.

responses.point: Ranked B008 first because bringing macroscopic mechanical oscillators to the quantum ground state and entangling and squeezing them addresses the quantum-classical boundary, but concedes that five credited names cannot fit into three and that the first ground-state demonstrations were near-simultaneous.
responses.response: I respect the fundamental motivation, and as a detector builder I value quantum-limited displacement sensing. But my objection is the one you raise yourself. With near-simultaneous milestones across microwave and optical platforms and five or more equally deserving people for three places, any trio is arbitrary, and I would not want an allocation that the committee could not defend. Two others ranking it only seventh and eighth suggest the committee shares that view. I am also not convinced the 2025 prize and this entry are cleanly separable in the public mind, so I rank it below B016 and B045.

responses.point: Ranked B026 circuit QED first as a clean basic quantum-optics advance on a chip that underlies superconducting processors, but flagged the 2025 overlap, the unsettled credit among Blais, Girvin, Huang, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, and his own possible conflict.
responses.response: I appreciate the transparency about your closeness to that community. My concern is timing and attribution. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits was awarded only a year ago, and a prompt second circuit prize for the same hardware family risks looking repetitive, even if cQED is physically distinct. I would also be uneasy about naming three of five plausible people when you yourself list Girvin and Huang as outside the credited names. I do not dismiss it, and the physics is mature, but I would rather it wait and that you consider recusing yourself from the final choice on B026.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree a two-person Halzen-Karle attribution for IceCube, given AMANDA predecessors and other collaboration leaders.
Whether to cite only the diffuse flux or also the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane), which await independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD.
How distinct the Katori-Ye lattice clock is from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which I cannot judge in detail outside my own field.
Whether the condensed-matter members can settle a defensible set of at most three names for B040 or B038.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to the credited IceCube candidates is apparent from my profile. I am an astroparticle physicist and work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, so IceCube is in a neighbouring field and I may have a taste bias toward detector-driven astroparticle results. I am not aware of a recusal-level tie, and I will recuse if a collaboration link emerges.
